title: Manthara on the rooftop
hook: a maid on a rooftop sees the lights, and the first person she tells is overjoyed for a son not her own
carry: sama-darshana: seeing everyone with equal eyes

segments.voice: Yesterday: a city lit for a pouring at dawn, the same abhisheka temples still offer. Your line was abhisheka, the pouring that honors the holy.

Valmiki doesn't tell us much about where she came from. She's a maid from Queen Kaikeyi's family household, and she has always lived beside Kaikeyi. Her name is Manthara. The text says her back is bent. On the night before the coronation, she happens to climb up to a high terrace, the way anyone might go up to the roof to see what the noise is about. And below her, the whole city is glowing.
screen: `A MAID FROM KAIKEYI'S FAMILY.` → `UP TO THE ROOF.` → `THE CITY IS GLOWING.`

segments.voice: Manthara sees banners, flowers, people in their best clothes, music in the streets. What's going on, she asks a nurse nearby. Why is Kausalya, Rama's mother, handing out gifts? The nurse, delighted, tells her: tomorrow the king will make Rama his heir. Manthara goes down the stairs in a fury. She finds Kaikeyi lying on her bed. Get up, she says. Something terrible is happening to you. The king is going to make Rama heir. Your good fortune is about to dry up like a river in summer. And here is the first surprise. Kaikeyi is glad. Truly glad. She sits up and gives Manthara a beautiful jewel as a reward for the news. Then she says the line that matters most. Rama and Bharata are the same to me. I see no difference between them. Hindus have a name for that kind of seeing: sama-darshana, equal vision. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the wise look with the same eyes on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person the world shuns, because the same Self lives in all of them. Tonight, Kaikeyi has that vision for two boys, her own son and another woman's. Quick retellings make her the wicked stepmother from her first scene. Valmiki doesn't. He shows her generous first, so that when she changes, you watch equal eyes go narrow. Manthara has heard all this. And she throws the jewel on the floor.
screen: `WHAT'S GOING ON DOWN THERE?` · `KAIKEYI IS GLAD, AND GIVES A JEWEL.` · `I SEE NO DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM.` · `SAMA-DARSHANA: EQUAL VISION.` · then, large: `SHE THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: Picture two people side by side: one you find easy to love, and one you don't. If you pray, say a blessing for both in the same breath; many Hindus close their prayers with sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy. If you don't pray, simply wish them both well, the same wish, on each breath out, and notice where the wish wants to be smaller for one of them.
Manthara. Kaikeyi's maid, who sees the coronation lights from a rooftop and brings the news, and whose mistress, at first, sees no difference between Rama and her own son.
Your line: sama-darshana, seeing everyone with equal eyes. Kaikeyi's first answer is gladness. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Manthara's name is sometimes used for someone who stirs up trouble in a family, but the Ayodhya Kanda is read closely enough that Kaikeyi's first, generous reaction is often pointed out.

fork.setup: you're Kaikeyi. your maid rushes in: the king will make Rama heir tomorrow. what do you feel first?
fork.reveal: Kaikeyi is delighted, gives Manthara a jewel, and says she sees no difference between Rama and Bharata: equal vision, for her own son and another's.

original.note: Sanskrit mantharā, the maid's name. the adjective manthara can mean slow or bent.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kaikeyi was the wicked stepmother all along.
what it means: in Valmiki, her first reaction to Rama's coronation is joy and a gift.
what a scholar hears: the text lets us watch Kaikeyi change over a few sargas, which is part of why commentators and retellers have argued for centuries about how much blame she carries.
